A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HOPS research, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends after the references; v2 includes Supplementary Material, Sections 6–12. Supplementary additions below mean newly available content in the supplied PDFs, not necessarily newly conducted experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original VPR experiments on RobotCar, Nordland and SFU-Mountain, dimensionality-reduction and synthetic-reference experiments, and dataset-identification outcomes.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and supplies additional original results, including AnyLoc comparisons, Google Landmarks compression, dataset-identification baselines and qualitative retrieval examples.

M1.justification: The descriptor summation, cosine-distance matching and optional Gaussian random projection remain unchanged. Section 3.3 clarifies that projection is used for the dimensionality experiment, while the supplement explains existing bundling applications. No new HOPS component or altered procedure is established.

E1.justification: Section 9 adds evaluation on Google Landmarks v2 micro, extending coverage from repeated route traversals to an unstructured collection with varying numbers of reference images per place. This substantially broadens the input environment tested. Dataset identification and the three original datasets were already covered in v1.

E2.justification: Figure 4 adds pooling and distance-matrix averaging to the dimensionality comparison. Tables 9–10 add one-image and ten-image dataset-identification baselines and maximum/median distance aggregation; minimum aggregation is also displayed and matches pooling. Table 8 adds a dimensionality-reduction compression comparator. Tables 5–7 supply the AnyLoc comparisons previously mentioned without results in v1.

E3.justification: The new Landmarks evaluation fuses 7–9 images per place, reducing 23,294 references to 3,103, and compares this with retaining all references at 1024 dimensions under a similar storage budget. Dataset-identification comparisons introduce one-reference and ten-reference sampling controls. These substantially extend the evaluation design; the original datasets' sampling counts and matching tolerances remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 5–10 expand dimensionality sensitivity analysis beyond v1's four-descriptor RobotCar Dusk example to all six main descriptors on six additional query sets. Figures 12–14 add successful and failed retrieval cases across the three original datasets, including failures where another method succeeds. These substantially expand sensitivity and error-analysis evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. v2's randomly selected dataset-identification baselines are reported without variability or repetition information.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their values, but v2 adds extensive numerical and qualitative results. For example, AnyLoc on RobotCar Dusk achieves 84.0 R@1 with HOPS versus 69.7 for the best single reference. The new Landmarks comparison reports 69.7 for original references, 65.8 after HOPS compression and 59.7 with 1024-dimensional references. Section 4.3 also corrects the exception count from two to three, acknowledging CosPlace Night's already-tabulated 19.4 versus 21.2.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6, the quasi-orthogonality reasoning, complexity statements and Johnson–Lindenstrauss motivation are retained. The supplement adds no formal theorem, proof, assumption or mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, principal contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about descriptor fusion, generalization, efficiency, synthetic references and dataset identification. The introduction clarifies that the quoted dimensionality reductions concern feature dimensions without materially redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: Section 9 interprets unstructured-reference compression as a storage and computation tradeoff with some recall loss. Section 12 attributes remaining failures mainly to visual similarity between geographically distant places. These add applicability qualifications while retaining the original explanations concerning feature reinforcement, nearby-match disambiguation and low-dimensional descriptors.

D1.justification: A HOPS repository address replaces v1's promise of code upon acceptance. The supplement specifies AnyLoc's author-released weights, 49,152-dimensional representation and omission of PCA, and identifies SALAD and cosine matching for dataset identification. Section 3.3 clarifies that core results use no random projection. These are additional disclosures, not evidence of changed implementations.

R1.justification: The related-work sections and 86-work bibliography are retained. Section 11 adds a focused comparison with the already-cited approaches in references 22 and 51, emphasizing differences in reference storage and query-descriptor computation. This modestly expands research positioning.

P1.justification: The main section order and most wording remain intact. Changes include localized clarification of random projection, additional cross-references, the corrected outlier paragraph, publication headers and an organized supplementary narrative. The added scientific material is not accompanied by an extensive rewrite of the original paper.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–10 and Figures 5–14, including multi-panel sensitivity plots, a dataset-identification diagram and three qualitative image galleries. Figure 4 gains comparator curves and a revised legend, while Figure 3's caption specifies error units. These substantially expand and refine the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's empirical support through multi-reference controls in the dimensionality plots, an unstructured compression benchmark, detailed dataset-identification comparisons and explicit failure examples. Previously referenced supplementary evidence becomes inspectable, making the benefits and limitations substantially easier to assess. Code access information and implementation clarifications further help reproducibility. Minor inconsistencies, such as Table 8's 8488/8448 descriptor dimensions, do not outweigh these gains.
